title: Automotive Suspension Compliance Using an Equivalent Spring-Loaded Axial Model
summary: An automotive suspension compliance problem using spring compression, axial-member elongation, load sharing, and deformation compatibility in an equivalent axial model.
courseTopic: Axial deformation, deformation compatibility, spring stiffness, member elongation, and rigid-body idealization
primaryMechanicsCompetencies: Axial deformation of rods and bolts
expectedStudentDeliverable: Context interpretation, simplified model, deformation calculations using the instructor reference model, final distance calculation, and a short mechanics-based interpretation.
geometryComplexity: Real automotive suspension context reduced to a 1D axial-member, rigid-plate, and spring idealization for analysis.
problemDeliverableType: Context interpretation, annotated idealization, deformation calculations, final distance, and mechanics-based interpretation.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference equivalent axial model with rigid plates, a linear spring, a central coupling rod, two side bolts, dimensions, and equal and opposite tensile loads.
problemStatement:
Automotive suspension systems support the vehicle body while allowing controlled relative motion between the wheel-side suspension and the chassis as the vehicle travels over road irregularities. The coil spring provides elastic support and compliance, while the shock absorber or damper controls oscillatory motion. Suspension links and mounting structures transfer the resulting forces between the wheel assembly and the vehicle body.

For this MEEN 305 problem, the complete suspension geometry is not analyzed directly. Instead, the real suspension is used to motivate a simplified equivalent axial model that isolates spring compression and elastic deformation of load-carrying members. This allows the deformation compatibility of a compliant mechanical assembly to be studied using standard Mechanics of Materials concepts.
engineeringGoal: Use a simplified equivalent mechanics model to determine how an applied load changes the separation between two reference locations, identify the dominant deformation contribution, and interpret what the result means for the compliance of the modeled suspension system.
